claim: Following new case management guidelines issued by the World Health Organization in 2010, individuals presenting with fever at a health clinic in sub-Saharan Africa have an increased chance of receiving a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) prior to receiving antimalarial treatment.
source: Following new case management guidelines issued by the World Health Organization in 2010, individuals presenting with fever at a health clinic in sub-Saharan Africa have an increased chance of receiving a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) prior to receiving antimalarial treatment (World Health Organization, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization 2015 guidelines

claim: In highly endemic areas, malaria infections are both common and frequently asymptomatic.
source: However, in highly endemic areas, malaria infections are both common and frequently asymptomatic (Bousema et al., 2014), meaning that for many patients presenting at health care facilities, their fever and parasitaemia are not causally related.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bousema et al., 2014

claim: For many patients presenting at health care facilities in highly endemic areas, their fever and parasitaemia are not causally related.
source: However, in highly endemic areas, malaria infections are both common and frequently asymptomatic (Bousema et al., 2014), meaning that for many patients presenting at health care facilities, their fever and parasitaemia are not causally related.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that malaria infections are frequently asymptomatic in endemic areas

claim: Routine case surveillance systems generally report the incidence of clinical malaria based on counts of febrile individuals with a presumed or confirmed malaria infection.
source: Routine case surveillance systems generally report the incidence of clinical malaria based on counts of febrile individuals with a presumed or confirmed malaria infection (World Health Organization, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization 2016

claim: If malaria infections in many RDT-positive fever cases are in fact asymptomatic, then the resulting case reports will over-represent clinical malaria, even where RDT testing is ubiquitous.
source: If the malaria infections in many of these cases are in fact asymptomatic then the resulting case reports will over-represent clinical malaria, even where RDT testing is ubiquitous, leading to an overestimation of morbidity due to malaria.
evidence: Logical inference about the consequences of asymptomatic infections being counted as clinical cases

claim: Fevers caused by another pathogen but coincident with a malaria infection will suffer a systematic under-reporting under RDT-based surveillance protocols.
source: Conversely, fevers caused by another pathogen but coincident with a malaria infection will suffer a systematic under-reporting under this protocol and consequently the disease burden of non-malarial febrile illness (NMFI) will be underestimated.
evidence: Logical inference about surveillance system biases

claim: Co-infections can simultaneously be the cause of fever in instances where a febrile individual has both a malaria infection and a NMFI.
source: In instances where a febrile individual has both a malaria infection and a NMFI, both infections can simultaneously be the cause of the fever.
evidence: Statement about the possibility of co-infections causing fever

claim: Co-infections have been known to modulate both the parasite load of both diseases and the severity of the individual's fever.
source: Indeed co-infections have been known to modulate both the parasite load of both diseases and the severity of the individual's fever (French et al., 2001; Hartgers and Yazdanbakhsh, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to French et al., 2001 and Hartgers and Yazdanbakhsh, 2006

claim: Symptoms of many non-malarial febrile illnesses can be non-specific and similar to malaria, including bacterial infections such as pneumonia and meningitis.
source: Diagnosing and treating NMFI is challenging as symptoms of many of these diseases can be non-specific and similar to malaria, for example bacterial infections such as pneumonia (Hildenwall et al., 2016; Källander et al., 2004) and meningitis (Gwer et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on pneumonia and meningitis

claim: Routine diagnostic tests have not yet been developed or are not commonplace for many non-malarial febrile illnesses.
source: Additionally, routine diagnostic tests have not yet been developed or are not commonplace for many of these diseases (Chappuis et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chappuis et al., 2013

claim: The rate of fever associated with (but not necessarily caused by) a malaria infection has been shown to have declined over time in some settings, halving between 1986 and 2007 in one collation of field studies.
source: The rate of fever associated with (but not necessarily caused by) a malaria infection has been shown to have declined over time in some settings, halving between 1986 and 2007 in one collation of field studies (D'Acremont et al., 2010); a trend likely driven by the declining prevalence of malaria over the latter portion of that time period.
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Acremont et al., 2010

claim: The decline in fever associated with malaria infection between 1986 and 2007 was likely driven by the declining prevalence of malaria over the latter portion of that time period.
source: The rate of fever associated with (but not necessarily caused by) a malaria infection has been shown to have declined over time in some settings, halving between 1986 and 2007 in one collation of field studies (D'Acremont et al., 2010); a trend likely driven by the declining prevalence of malaria over the latter portion of that time period.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the cause of the observed trend

claim: Attempts have been made to measure the malaria-attributable fraction arithmetically using case-control trials, where the difference in the rate of malaria positivity in febrile and afebrile individuals is used to calculate the attributable fraction.
source: Attempts have been made to measure the malaria-attributable fraction arithmetically using case-control trials, where the difference in the rate of malaria positivity in febrile and afebrile individuals is used to calculate the attributable fraction (Ehrhardt et al., 2006; Schellenberg et al., 1994; Smith et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple case-control studies

claim: Logistic regression approaches have been developed to estimate causal fractions based on measurements of blood parasite density.
source: Alternatively, logistic regression approaches have been developed to estimate causal fractions based on measurements of blood parasite density.
evidence: Statement about methodological approaches in the literature

claim: Logistic regression approaches for estimating malaria-attributable fractions have been demonstrated in various settings in Kenya.
source: This approach has been demonstrated in numerous field trials, including various settings in Kenya (Afrane et al., 2014; Bloland et al., 1999), in an area of seasonal transmission in Burkina Faso (Bisoffi et al., 2010), and in a national survey in Mozambique (Mabunda et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in Kenya

claim: Logistic regression approaches for estimating malaria-attributable fractions have been demonstrated in an area of seasonal transmission in Burkina Faso.
source: This approach has been demonstrated in numerous field trials, including various settings in Kenya (Afrane et al., 2014; Bloland et al., 1999), in an area of seasonal transmission in Burkina Faso (Bisoffi et al., 2010), and in a national survey in Mozambique (Mabunda et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to study in Burkina Faso

claim: Logistic regression approaches for estimating malaria-attributable fractions have been demonstrated in a national survey in Mozambique.
source: This approach has been demonstrated in numerous field trials, including various settings in Kenya (Afrane et al., 2014; Bloland et al., 1999), in an area of seasonal transmission in Burkina Faso (Bisoffi et al., 2010), and in a national survey in Mozambique (Mabunda et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to study in Mozambique

claim: Computational simulations of malaria transmission can be adapted to estimate an upper bound on the malaria-attributable fraction of fevers at varying levels of Plasmodium falciparum prevalence.
source: Computational simulations of malaria transmission can also be adapted to estimate an upper bound on the malaria-attributable fraction of fevers at varying levels of Plasmodium falciparum prevalence (PfPR), by monitoring the proportion of parasite-positive individuals within a simulation with a symptomatic infection (here, a symptomatic infection is synonymous with a malaria attributable fever, as co-infections with other pathogens are not typically simulated) (Griffin et al., 2010; Ross et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Griffin et al., 2010 and Ross et al., 2006

claim: The study used a total of 38 household surveys in 24 sub-Saharan African countries collected between 2006 and 2014.
source: Using a total of 38 household surveys in 24 Saharan African countries collected between 2006 and 2014, we collated 155,369 observations of two-week fever prevalence and RDT diagnostic outcome for P. falciparum in children from 10,606 locations with two modelled predictor variables: P. falciparum prevalence in children under five years of age (PfPR0-5); and suitability for fever without a malaria infection.
evidence: Description of the data used in the study

claim: The study collated 155,369 observations of two-week fever prevalence and RDT diagnostic outcome for P. falciparum in children from 10,606 locations.
source: Using a total of 38 household surveys in 24 Saharan African countries collected between 2006 and 2014, we collated 155,369 observations of two-week fever prevalence and RDT diagnostic outcome for P. falciparum in children from 10,606 locations with two modelled predictor variables: P. falciparum prevalence in children under five years of age (PfPR0-5); and suitability for fever without a malaria infection.
evidence: Description of the data used in the study

claim: In 2014, the prevalence of fever of any cause across the stable limits of P. falciparum transmission was 31.0%.
source: In 2014, the prevalence of fever of any cause across the stable limits of P. falciparum transmission was 31.0%, and increased slightly over the study period, from 27.0% in 2006.
evidence: Model-derived estimate for 2014

claim: All-cause fever prevalence increased slightly over the study period, from 27.0% in 2006 to 31.0% in 2014.
source: In 2014, the prevalence of fever of any cause across the stable limits of P. falciparum transmission was 31.0%, and increased slightly over the study period, from 27.0% in 2006.
evidence: Model-derived temporal trend

claim: Niger (53.4%), Gabon (44.9%) and Nigeria (42.8%) had the highest all-cause fever prevalence in 2014.
source: Countries were highly heterogeneous in their overall fever burden, with Niger (53.4%), Gabon (44.9%) and Nigeria (42.8%) having the highest all-cause fever prevalence in 2014.
evidence: Model-derived country-specific estimates for 2014

claim: Swaziland (4.60%), Eritrea (5.3%) and Somalia (10.1%) had the lowest all-cause fever prevalence in 2014.
source: The countries with the lowest fever burden in the same year were Swaziland (4.60%), Eritrea (5.3%) and Somalia (10.1%)
evidence: Model-derived country-specific estimates for 2014

claim: In 2014, less than one-third (28.0%) of all fevers in P. falciparum malaria-infected children under five were attributable to P. falciparum in any given two-week period.
source: In 2014, we estimate that less than one-third (28.0%) of all fevers in P. falciparum malaria-infected children under five were attributable to P. falciparum in any given two-week period.
evidence: Model-derived estimate for 2014

claim: Swaziland (86.9%), Eritrea (81.9%) and Somalia (69.9%) had the largest contribution of MAF to malaria-positive fevers in 2014.
source: This fraction varied geographically, as shown in Figure 2, with the largest contribution of MAF to malaria-positive fevers in 2014 in Swaziland (86.9%), Eritrea (81.9%) and Somalia (69.9%) and the lowest in Niger (14.7%), Gabon (20.9%) and Nigeria (20.9%).
evidence: Model-derived country-specific estimates for 2014

claim: Niger (14.7%), Gabon (20.9%) and Nigeria (20.9%) had the lowest contribution of MAF to malaria-positive fevers in 2014.
source: This fraction varied geographically, as shown in Figure 2, with the largest contribution of MAF to malaria-positive fevers in 2014 in Swaziland (86.9%), Eritrea (81.9%) and Somalia (69.9%) and the lowest in Niger (14.7%), Gabon (20.9%) and Nigeria (20.9%).
evidence: Model-derived country-specific estimates for 2014

claim: The fraction of malaria-positive fevers attributable to malaria varied through time, decreasing continent-wide from 36.1% in 2006 to 28.0% in 2014.
source: The fraction also varied though time, decreasing continent-wide from 36.1% in 2006 to 28.0% in 2014.
evidence: Model-derived temporal trend

claim: Age of the child was shown to have an effect on the likelihood of a child developing a malaria-attributable fever.
source: Age of the child was also shown to have an effect on the likelihood of a child developing a malaria-attributable fever.
evidence: Model-derived finding about age effects

claim: For all children under five, the probability of an attributable fever grew with PfPR0-5, with a decreasing gradient as PfPR0-5 increases.
source: For all children, the probability of an attributable fever grew with PfPR0-5, with a decreasing gradient as PfPR0-5 increases.
evidence: Model-derived relationship shown in Figure 4a

claim: The probability of a malaria-attributable fever increases linearly with PfPR0-5 for children under two years of age.
source: Figure 4b shows that this trend is also true for children over two years of age, but the probability of a malaria-attributable fever increases linearly with PfPR0-5 for children under two years of age.
evidence: Model-derived relationship shown in Figure 4b

claim: In 2014, 35.7% of all fevers in children under five were accompanied by an RDT-patent P. falciparum infection.
source: In 2014, we estimate that 35.7% of all fevers in children under five were accompanied by an RDT-patent P. falciparum infection, and that this fraction has declined from 48.5% in 2006.
evidence: Model-derived estimate for 2014

claim: The fraction of all fevers accompanied by an RDT-patent P. falciparum infection declined from 48.5% in 2006 to 35.7% in 2014.
source: In 2014, we estimate that 35.7% of all fevers in children under five were accompanied by an RDT-patent P. falciparum infection, and that this fraction has declined from 48.5% in 2006.
evidence: Model-derived temporal trend

claim: The Central African Republic (71.0%), Equatorial Guinea (66.2%) and Guinea (65.7%) had the highest proportion of malaria-positive fevers in 2014.
source: The countries with the highest proportion of malaria-positive fevers in 2014 were the Central African Republic (71.0%), Equatorial Guinea (66.2%) and Guinea (65.7%) and the lowest were Ethiopia (1.4%), Botswana (1.6%) and Swaziland (2.9%).
evidence: Model-derived country-specific estimates for 2014

claim: Ethiopia (1.4%), Botswana (1.6%) and Swaziland (2.9%) had the lowest proportion of malaria-positive fevers in 2014.
source: The countries with the highest proportion of malaria-positive fevers in 2014 were the Central African Republic (71.0%), Equatorial Guinea (66.2%) and Guinea (65.7%) and the lowest were Ethiopia (1.4%), Botswana (1.6%) and Swaziland (2.9%).
evidence: Model-derived country-specific estimates for 2014

claim: In 2014, 35.7% of all fevers were accompanied by a malaria infection, but only 28.0% of those (10.0% of all fevers) were causally attributable to malaria.
source: We estimate that 35.7% of all self-reported fevers were accompanied by a malaria infection in 2014, but that only 28.0% of those (10.0% of all fevers) were causally attributable to malaria.
evidence: Model-derived estimates for 2014 presented in the abstract

claim: Most fevers among malaria-positive children are caused by non-malaria illnesses.
source: Most fevers among malaria-positive children are therefore caused by non-malaria illnesses.
evidence: Inference from the finding that only 28.0% of malaria-positive fevers are attributable to malaria

claim: The fraction of all fevers that are due to NMFI increased over the study period, from 82.5% in 2006 to 90.0% in 2014.
source: The fraction of all fevers that are due to NMFI increased over the study period, from 82.5% in 2006 to 90.0% in 2014.
evidence: Model-derived temporal trend

claim: Ethiopia (99.4%), Botswana (99.2%) and Gambia (98.5%) had the largest fractions of NMFI to all fevers in 2014.
source: The countries with the largest fractions of NMFI to all fevers were Ethiopia (99.4%), Botswana (99.2%) and Gambia (98.5%), and the smallest were Guinea (58.2%), Equatorial Guinea (60.4%) and Central African Republic (64.6%).
evidence: Model-derived country-specific estimates for 2014

claim: Guinea (58.2%), Equatorial Guinea (60.4%) and Central African Republic (64.6%) had the smallest fractions of NMFI to all fevers in 2014.
source: The countries with the largest fractions of NMFI to all fevers were Ethiopia (99.4%), Botswana (99.2%) and Gambia (98.5%), and the smallest were Guinea (58.2%), Equatorial Guinea (60.4%) and Central African Republic (64.6%).
evidence: Model-derived country-specific estimates for 2014

claim: The proportion of MCF within NMFI fell over the study period, from 37.6% in 2006 to 28.6% in 2014.
source: The proportion of MCF within NMFI fell over the study period, from 37.6% in 2006, to 28.6% in 2014.
evidence: Model-derived temporal trend

claim: The Central African Republic (55.2%), Burkina Faso (54.9%) and Equatorial Guinea (44.2%) had the highest prevalence of MCF within NMFI in 2014.
source: The countries that had the highest prevalence of MCF within NMFI were the Central African Republic (55.2%), Burkina Faso (54.9%) and Equatorial Guinea (44.2%), and the countries with the lowest prevalence of MCF within NMFI were Swaziland (0.4%), Botswana (0.8%) and Ethiopia (0.8%).
evidence: Model-derived country-specific estimates for 2014

claim: Swaziland (0.4%), Botswana (0.8%) and Ethiopia (0.8%) had the lowest prevalence of MCF within NMFI in 2014.
source: The countries that had the highest prevalence of MCF within NMFI were the Central African Republic (55.2%), Burkina Faso (54.9%) and Equatorial Guinea (44.2%), and the countries with the lowest prevalence of MCF within NMFI were Swaziland (0.4%), Botswana (0.8%) and Ethiopia (0.8%).
evidence: Model-derived country-specific estimates for 2014

claim: The majority of febrile illness in Africa is caused by pathogens other than P. falciparum malaria, even in areas where malaria is highly endemic.
source: The majority of febrile illness in Africa is caused by pathogens other than P. falciparum malaria, even in areas where malaria is highly endemic, and the proportion of all fevers caused by NMFI has risen since 2006.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from model results

claim: Over a typical two-week period in 2014, one in four children under five years old residing in the limits of stable malaria transmission will suffer a fever not caused by P. falciparum malaria.
source: We estimate here that over a typical two-week period in 2014 one in four children under five years old residing in the limits of stable malaria transmission will suffer a fever not caused by P. falciparum malaria, whereas only one in every 32 children will suffer a fever directly caused by P. falciparum.
evidence: Model-derived estimate for 2014

claim: Over a typical two-week period in 2014, only one in every 32 children under five years old residing in the limits of stable malaria transmission will suffer a fever directly caused by P. falciparum.
source: We estimate here that over a typical two-week period in 2014 one in four children under five years old residing in the limits of stable malaria transmission will suffer a fever not caused by P. falciparum malaria, whereas only one in every 32 children will suffer a fever directly caused by P. falciparum.
evidence: Model-derived estimate for 2014

claim: Current estimations of malaria burden in Africa based on RDT-positive cases of fever may be overestimating the burden by up to two-thirds.
source: We show that current estimations of malaria burden in Africa based on RDT-positive cases of fever may be overestimating the burden by up to two-thirds, and the level of overestimation is likely to be highly heterogeneous between different countries (Figure 3).
evidence: Inference from model results about surveillance system biases

claim: Countries such as Niger, Gabon and Nigeria, where fewer than 21% of malaria-positive fever cases are causally attributable to malaria, may be substantially overestimating the morbidity caused by malaria.
source: For example, countries such as Niger, Gabon and Nigeria, where fewer than 21% of malaria-positive fever cases are causally attributable to malaria, may be substantially overestimating the morbidity caused by malaria (and systematically underestimating the burden of other diseases that may be co-infecting and causal).
evidence: Inference from model results for specific countries

claim: A substantial proportion of RDT-positive fevers are likely to be coincident with and caused by a NMFI.
source: Additionally, these results have implications for the effectiveness of treatment received at point of care, as a substantial proportion of RDT-positive fevers are likely to be coincident with and caused by a NMFI.
evidence: Inference from model results about clinical implications

claim: The estimations of MAF prevalence in the past two weeks are comparable to estimations of clinical incidence from an ensemble of transmission models.
source: Our estimations of MAF prevalence in the past two weeks are comparable to estimations of clinical incidence from an ensemble of transmission models (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Cameron et al., 2015) although our estimates match more closely to transmission model estimations of the prevalence of febrile illness lasting the duration of the past two-to-four weeks, rather than the past zero-to-two.
evidence: Comparison with external transmission model estimates

claim: Children in 13 household surveys had a fever for on average 5.38 days (±3.85 days) prior to the interview.
source: For 13 of the 38 household surveys used in this analysis, the number of days since the onset of the child's fever was available. Children in these surveys had a fever for on average 5.38 days (±3.85 days) prior to the interview.
evidence: Descriptive statistics from survey data

claim: The total number of fever cases accompanied by an RDT-patent P. falciparum infection declined substantially over the study period (from 48.5% in 2006 to 35.7% in 2014), linked with declining PfPR0-5 over the same time.
source: The total number of fever cases accompanied by an RDT-patent P. falciparum infection declined substantially over the study period (from 48.5% in 2006 to 35.7% in 2014), linked with declining PfPR0-5 over the same time (Bhatt et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: Model-derived temporal trend linked to declining prevalence

claim: Gabon was the only country with a noteworthy increase in malaria-positive fevers over the study period.
source: The only country with a noteworthy increase in malaria-positive fevers over the study period was Gabon, which also experienced an increase in PfPR0-5 between 2006 and 2014.
evidence: Model-derived country-specific temporal trend

claim: Gabon experienced an increase in PfPR0-5 between 2006 and 2014.
source: The only country with a noteworthy increase in malaria-positive fevers over the study period was Gabon, which also experienced an increase in PfPR0-5 between 2006 and 2014.
evidence: Observation from prevalence data

claim: No previous attempts have been made to measure childhood fever prevalence (and the malaria/non-malaria causality of the fever) from surveys recording two-week fever history.
source: This modelling approach makes use of household survey datasets in a novel way; no previous attempts have been made to measure childhood fever prevalence (and the malaria/non-malaria causality of the fever) from surveys recording two-week fever history.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the methodological approach

claim: The accuracy of two-week recall of fever from the child's caregiver can be subject to biases such as length of time since the fever, the child's frequency of febrile episodes, the economic status of the family, and even the child's sex.
source: This approach has some drawbacks: it relies on two-week recall of fever from the child's caregiver, the accuracy of which can be subject to biases such as (i) length of time since the fever; (ii) the child's frequency of febrile episodes, (iii) the economic status of the family, and (iv) even the child's sex (Das et al., 2012; Rockers and McConnell, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on recall bias

claim: Fever caused by P. vivax malaria is included as a NMFI by definition in this study.
source: We also include fever caused by P. vivax malaria as a NMFI by definition, as not all household surveys tested for P. vivax with RDT and thus only P. falciparum outcomes were used in this analysis.
evidence: Methodological decision described in the manuscript

claim: P. vivax is unlikely to have a major effect on most of Africa due to high Duffy negativity resulting in unstable P. vivax transmission, and very low levels of stable transmission in Madagascar and the horn of Africa.
source: This is unlikely to have a major effect on most of Africa due to high Duffy negativity resulting in unstable P. vivax transmission, and very low levels of stable transmission in Madagascar and the horn of Africa (Gething et al., 2012; Howes et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on P. vivax distribution

claim: The low prevalence of malaria-positive fevers at all levels of P. falciparum endemicity suggests that passive case detection alone may not be enough to halt transmission of malaria.
source: The low prevalence of malaria-positive fevers at all levels of P. falciparum endemicity suggests that passive case detection alone may not be enough to halt transmission of malaria, as many infected children are afebrile at any one time (regardless of whether their fever is attributable to the malaria infection or not).
evidence: Inference from model results about malaria control strategies

claim: Children under two years of age have a higher probability of developing a malaria-attributable fever than children older than two in areas where PfPR0-5 is greater than 30%.
source: We find that the relationship between MAF prevalence and PfPR is not equivalent across all age groups (Figure 4), with children under two years of age having a higher probability of developing a malaria-attributable fever than children older than two in areas where PfPR0-5 is greater than 30%.
evidence: Model-derived age-stratified relationship shown in Figure 4

claim: For older children living in high PfPR locations, a higher proportion of the population will have acquired immunity to malaria infection.
source: For older children living in high PfPR locations, a higher proportion of the population will have acquired immunity to malaria infection (Doolan et al., 2009), and therefore may be less likely to present with a malaria-attributable fever.
evidence: Supported by citation to Doolan et al., 2009 on acquired immunity

claim: All malaria-endemic countries now adopt the official policy of parasite-based diagnosis of suspected malaria cases before issuing antimalarials.
source: Despite all malaria-endemic countries now adopting the official policy of parasite-based diagnosis of suspected malaria cases before issuing antimalarials, a large number of suspected malaria cases still do not receive a diagnostic test before treatment (Hertz et al., 2013; World Health Organization, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hertz et al., 2013 and World Health Organization, 2015

claim: The proportion of suspected malaria cases not receiving a diagnostic test before treatment decreased from 64% in 2005 to 35% in 2014.
source: This proportion has decreased over the time period of this study, from 64% of suspected cases not receiving a diagnostic test in 2005 to only 35% in 2014 (World Health Organization, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2015

claim: The high proportion of suspected cases not receiving parasite-based diagnosis lies predominantly in resource limitation in rural health clinics in malaria endemic countries.
source: The reasons for this high proportion of suspected cases not receiving parasite-based diagnosis lies predominantly in resource limitation in rural health clinics in malaria endemic countries (Ghai et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ghai et al., 2016

claim: The Worldwide Antimalarial Resistance Network (WWARN) collects clinical evidence of non-malarial febrile illness (NMFI) caused by neglected tropical diseases from peer-reviewed case studies of fever diagnoses from across the malaria-endemic world.
source: The Worldwide Antimalarial Resistance Network (WWARN) now collects clinical evidence of non-malarial febrile illness (NMFI) caused by neglected tropical diseases from peer-reviewed case studies of fever diagnoses from across the malaria-endemic world (Worldwide Antimalarial Resistance Network, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to WWARN, 2017

claim: A major review of 146 case studies in the Mekong region of Southeast Asia showed that misdiagnosis and mistreatment of fever was a common outcome for individuals who were co-infected with malaria and other diseases with overlapping symptoms.
source: For example, a major review of 146 case studies in the Mekong region of Southeast Asia (Acestor et al., 2012), showed that misdiagnosis and mistreatment of the fever was a common outcome for individuals who were co-infected with malaria and other diseases with overlapping symptoms (e.g., Dengue fever virus, Orientia tsutsugamushi and Rickettsia species).
evidence: Supported by citation to Acestor et al., 2012

claim: Current WHO guidelines for integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI) is currently suboptimal for the treatment of non-malarial fever.
source: In addition to implicating potential overestimation of the burden of malaria in the past, the results of this study suggest that current WHO guidelines for integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI) is currently suboptimal for the treatment of non-malarial fever.
evidence: Inference from study results about clinical guidelines

claim: Thirty-eight cross sectional, nationally-representative georeferenced surveys of malaria prevalence in children less than five years of age across 24 countries in sub-Saharan Africa were obtained from the Malaria Atlas Project database.
source: Thirty-eight cross sectional, nationally-representative georeferenced surveys of malaria prevalence in children less than five years of age across 24 countries in sub-Saharan Africa were obtained from the Malaria Atlas Project database (Guerra et al., 2007; Malaria Atlas Project , 2017).
evidence: Description of data sources

claim: In the household surveys, a blood sample was taken from any children present and tested for malaria parasites with both a RDT and Giemsa-stained microscopy.
source: In these surveys, a blood sample was taken from any children present and tested for malaria parasites with both a RDT and Giemsa-stained microscopy.
evidence: Description of survey methodology

claim: RDT-derived diagnostic outcome was used as an indicator of malaria positivity within the last two weeks, to lessen the possibility of a recent infection having been cleared via artemisinin combination therapy.
source: Here, we used the RDT-derived diagnostic outcome as an indicator of malaria positivity within the last two weeks, to lessen the possibility of a recent infection having been cleared via artemisinin combination therapy (ACT) (and therefore presenting as a negative result by microscopy).
evidence: Methodological decision explained in the manuscript

claim: RDTs offer a more accurate representation of two-week infection than microscopy due to the persistence of histidine-rich protein II in the blood for up to 14 days after parasite clearance with ACT.
source: RDTs offer a more accurate representation of two-week infection than microscopy due to the persistence of histidine-rich protein II in the blood for up to 14 days after parasite clearance with ACT (Mayxay et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayxay et al., 2001

claim: Diagnostic and fever history outcomes from a total of 155,369 children were aggregated within 5 × 5 km raster cells, resulting in a total 10,606 data points.
source: Diagnostic and fever history outcomes from a total of 155,369 children that were aggregated within 5 × 5 km raster cells, resulting in a total 10,606 data points.
evidence: Description of data processing

claim: The PfPR0-5 covariate was generated for each year using the PfPR2-10 modelled predictions of slide-patent African PfPR from the Malaria Atlas Project, age-standardised to 0–5 years.
source: The PfPR0-5 covariate was generated for each year using the PfPR2-10 modelled predictions of slide-patent African PfPR from the Malaria Atlas Project (Bhatt et al., 2015), age-standardised to 0–5 years using the 'agestand' package in R, based on a previously described age-standardisation procedure for PfPR (Smith et al., 2007), and transformed to predict RDT-based prevalence via an microscopy-to-RDT relationship identified in earlier work (Mappin et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of covariate generation methodology

claim: Prior to this study, no mapped estimates of environmental suitability for background fever existed for the African continent.
source: Prior to this study, no mapped estimates of environmental suitability for background fever existed for the African continent, hence a modelled estimate of environmental suitability for background fever was constructed using a boosted regression tree (BRT) model.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the background fever suitability covariate

claim: A boosted regression tree (BRT) model was used to construct a modelled estimate of environmental suitability for background fever.
source: Prior to this study, no mapped estimates of environmental suitability for background fever existed for the African continent, hence a modelled estimate of environmental suitability for background fever was constructed using a boosted regression tree (BRT) model.
evidence: Description of modeling methodology

claim: The BRT approach generates a flexible regression model by recursively splitting response data by predictor variables and then combining regression tree models to reduce overall predictive deviance.
source: The BRT approach generates a flexible regression model in two steps. Initially, response data are split recursively by predictor variables, where predictor variables that maximise the partitioned response data's homogeneity are selected more frequently in subsequent steps. This is followed by a 'boosting' step, where the regression tree models are combined to reduce the model's overall predictive deviance (Elith et al., 2008), and at each iterative step cross-validated against a randomly held-out subset to avoid overfitting (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Description of BRT methodology with citations

source: A large suite of potential environmental and socio-demographic covariates was assembled, as described elsewhere (Weiss et al., 2015). Briefly, 5 × 5 km resolution surfaces across the African continent of different environmental and sociodemographic covariate types—elevation, land cover, population density, precipitation, enhanced vegetation index (EVI), land surface temperature (LST), P. falciparum temperature suitability index (TSI) (Weiss et al., 2014), tasselled cap wetness (TCW), tasselled cap brightness (TCB), nighttime lights, Global Urban Footprint (Esch et al., 2012), and national-level World Bank indicators of poverty and healthcare quality (World Bank, 2017)—were obtained from the Malaria Atlas Project database and leveraged by constructing pixel-level spatial summaries (maximum, mean, minimum, standard deviation and range).
